keyQuestions.text: How do OpenBot routines (sentence form, time and event starts, act or tell, until an outcome) and the other repos' schedulers map onto skilled bots' cron, queue and git-hook triggers, and what is the smallest change that closes the gap?

Which OpenBot parts does a small team not need (enterprise, multi-tenant, Kubernetes, managed upgrades, mobile), which code in the eight repos can be reused directly under its license, and what ranked build order should a first build packet follow?
How should a routine's until outcome be evaluated after each run from an existing BOT.md precheck or stop expression, without adding a scheduler?
What is the smallest deterministic sentence-to-trigger planner that maps routine text onto cron, queue and git-hook kinds?
How should missed routine windows and a 15-minute floor map onto launchd calendar entries and the queue drain's retry bound?
Which OpenBot routine guardrails, the 20-enabled cap and failure-streak auto-off, belong in run records and the status index for a small team?

keyFindings.text: A single New-routine screen writes three stores through one planner: act-on-schedule with no outcome is a routine, act-on-schedule with an outcome is a goal plus a routine, act-on-event is a goal with a subscription, now-once is a goal run at once, and tell-only is a check-in. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/routines/plan.ts:73-151]

Buzz implements event-start automation as a YAML-as-code workflow engine with four trigger types (message posted, reaction added, schedule, webhook), seven actions including request-approval and delay, and a cron loop that ticks every 60 seconds with window-based matching. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/ARCHITECTURE.md:625-670]

Hermes Muse implements standing work as owned cron jobs with fixed cron keys and default expressions, driven by a script entry that builds a packet and lets the host run the model; a drain job batches work and re-wakes itself, and each watch job embeds its check and stop condition in the prompt. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/install.py:40-55] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/install.py:135-137] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/hooks.py:163]

OpenBot fires routines inside the server process: one server holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock and looks every 30 seconds, every server claims five turns at a time, and each firing is claimed from the shared work queue under a key naming its due minute so two servers cannot double-fire it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:147-161]

OpenBot surrounds the scheduler with product guardrails: a 15-minute floor per routine, a 20-enabled-routine cap per person, one failure message per failure streak and auto-off after ten consecutive failures, and missed windows skipped rather than replayed. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:107-145]

OpenBot treats a routine as one standing instruction read as a sentence in four parts: what it is, what starts it, whether it acts or only tells, and until what happens. Routines, goals and check-ins are drawn as one list although they remain three server stores. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:3-22]

OpenBot's "starts" admits a schedule, an event subscription, or a single now-run; "does" is act-within-approvals or tell-only; "until" is "you stop it" or a stated outcome that completes a goal. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:39-44] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:36-49]

Skilled bots already has the execution substrate a routine needs: a named file queue with rename-based single-claim and a three-attempt retry bound, a git-hook trigger that enqueues one request per matching bot on post-commit, and manual `bots run`/`bots enqueue`/`bots drain` verbs. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:1-20] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:43] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:189-201] [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:23-41]

Skilled bots' BOT.md admits exactly four trigger kinds — cron, queue, git-hook and manual — with no sentence form, no act-versus-tell field, no "until" outcome and no event subscription beyond the repository post-commit hook; cron is translated only into launchd calendar dictionaries or refused with a named invariant id. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:25-32] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:5-10] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:267-303]

The smallest gap-closing change is a routine layer that compiles to the existing four triggers rather than a new scheduler: an optional `routine` block in BOT.md (what, starts[], does, until), a deterministic sentence-to-block planner for the common schedule and event phrasings, `does: tell` mapped to local-only delivery plus a needs-you note, and `until` evaluated after each run from a precheck or stop expression; fatigue counting and missed-slot skipping attach to the existing run record and queue slot accounting. [INFERENCE: based on findings 4-9; OpenBot's scheduler, stores and UI are not needed, because the queue, git-hook and launchd paths already fire and claim work]

Directly liftable routine code exists in permissive repositories: OpenBot's `app/src/lib/routines/plan.ts` and `shared/routine-firing.ts` (MIT), OpenMausBot's `server/routine-schedules.ts`, `server/routine-cron-text.ts` and `server/routine-wake-retry.ts` (Apache-2.0), and Rakazo's `packages/core/src/routines/schedule.ts` (Apache-2.0). [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/app/src/lib/routines/plan.ts:73-151] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/shared/routine-firing.ts:52-79] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/server/routine-schedules.ts:1-30] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/server/routine-cron-text.ts:39-52] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/server/routine-wake-retry.ts:1-37] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/rakazo-main/packages/core/src/routines/schedule.ts:1-30]

Kubernetes is a second deployment shape with two Helm charts, a management agent, release-manifest promotion and GitOps output; it exists to give each person a computer and to scale the API apart from browsers, neither of which a small team needs. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/deployment.md:212-225] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/kubernetes-upgrades.md:1-5]

License matrix: OpenBot, OpenGhost and Hermes Muse are MIT; OpenMausBot, Rakazo, Turnstone and Buzz are Apache-2.0; openhuman is GPL-3.0. OpenMausBot's Apache-2.0 grant excludes everything under `enterprise/`, which is source-available under a separate enterprise license. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/LICENSE:1-2] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/LICENSE:2-3] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/LICENSING.md:1-12] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/rakazo-main/LICENSE:1-2] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/LICENSE:1-2] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/LICENSE:1-2] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/LICENSE:1-2] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/LICENSE:2-3] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/buzz-main/LICENSE:2-3]

Managed upgrades are a fleet feature: a management agent heartbeats to CopilotKit, Flux installs named releases inside a maintenance window, and every database-migrating upgrade needs a verified backup; a small team can upgrade by hand and skip all of it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/managed-upgrades.md:3-6] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/managed-upgrades.md:31-50] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/managed-upgrades.md:125-169]

Mobile is a separate Expo/React Native app with a deliberately limited launch scope (three focus areas, no Computer screen), so terminal-first parity does not need it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/app-guidelines.md:3] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/app-guidelines.md:74-108]

OpenBot ships as one container carrying the app, the API and Chromium, with either an external PostgreSQL or an embedded one, so a small team can run the whole product on one host with no cluster. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/deployment.md:3-17]

OpenBot's supervisor is what gives each person or isolated bot its own container; without it every bot shares one computer, which the deployment doc calls fine for one team trusting its bots and explicitly not fine as a tenant boundary. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/deployment.md:66-71]

Other liftable pieces target the other seven parts: OpenGhost's hook-compatible rules engine for approvals (MIT), Hermes Muse's owned-job table and watch prompt for routines (MIT), and Turnstone's output-guard judge for activity/approval review (Apache-2.0). [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/rules.js:1-10] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/hermes_muse/install.py:40-55] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/turnstone-main/turnstone/core/output_guard_judge.py:1-30]

Ranked build order for a first build packet: (1) routine block plus deterministic planner and routine list, (2) approvals inbox and activity feed over the existing needs-you items and run records, (3) terminal conversation with per-bot memory, (4) memory and skill mapping onto Skilled skills and spec-kit, (5) apps and secret vault over MCP and Code Mode, (6) per-bot computer exposure over worktrees, (7) small-team sign-in and roles only when a shared host is used. The first three reuse existing substrate; conversation and memory are the largest new surfaces; the last item is deferred until a second person shares a host. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-9 and the trigger, needs-you and run-record substrate read in iteration 1]

The team edition adds one "Everyone" admin scope above "Every Bot" and "This Bot", with admin pages for the same eight primitives plus vault and team; a few people on one machine do not need that policy layer. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:124-131] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:145-154]

`runPrecheck` is a reusable command executor: it runs `/bin/sh -c` in its own process group, treats a non-zero exit as a named failure, treats `[SILENT]` as a skip, and kills the whole group on timeout. The same helper can evaluate an `until` command after a run without new process plumbing. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/runner.ts:529-578]

OpenBot completes a goal when its stated outcome is met and switches off the routines that run it; a small-team routine layer needs only that same met transition for its own schedule, not the goal store or the multi-routine switch-off graph. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:76-92]

The `precheck` field itself must not be reused as the `until` field: its `[SILENT]` marker means "skip this run", not "the outcome is met", so sharing the helper is correct while sharing the field would invert the meaning of a successful check. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/runner.ts:568] [INFERENCE: based on the precheck call site at runner.ts:931-935]

The existing `precheck` field is a pre-dispatch gate: a non-zero exit or a `[SILENT]` marker skips the run entirely, so it cannot express an outcome that is evaluated after work has happened. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:69] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/runner.ts:931-935]

The run record already carries the exit reason, dispatch snapshot, skipped-slot summary and held slot, so a completion stamp belongs on that record rather than in a new store. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/run-record.ts:82-110] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/run-record.ts:130-141]

The smallest change is an optional `until` command on BOT.md, evaluated with the existing precheck runner only after a successful run: exit 0 means met, which sets a completion switch and records `untilMetAt`, while a non-zero exit means not met and the routine keeps its schedule. Size S (one schema field, one post-run call, one switch value, one status line), risk low because no scheduler, queue or launchd code changes. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-6]

The stop-switch layer already keeps a disable file outside every checkout, reads a damaged file as still set, and lets `bots enable` clear it; an until-met transition can reuse that layer instead of inventing a second stop mechanism. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/switches.ts:1-10] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/switches.ts:56-76]

The terminal outcome is finalized in `runBot` after `runSeeded` returns, and the terminal record is written before delivery starts, so an until evaluation has a natural insertion point between the two. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/runner.ts:750-757]

A smaller v1 that keeps the single-trigger invariant is possible: one cron or one queue/git-hook start per routine, with `starts` rendered as a list of names. That is size S but leaves OpenBot's "a routine can have more than one start" gap open, so it is a fallback rather than the recommended target. [INFERENCE: based on finding 6]

Combining those two permissive implementations gives a deterministic sentence-to-cron bridge for a closed phrase set (every day, weekdays, weekly, monthly, yearly, interval), with raw cron passthrough for anything else; this mirrors OpenBot's own split, where the form covers common schedules and a Bot handles the rest conversationally. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:36-57] [INFERENCE: based on findings 2 and 3]

Event starts are a name-mapping problem, not natural-language parsing: "when a pull request opens" maps to the existing git-hook trigger or a named queue, and "when an email arrives" maps to a queue name that a future mail connector feeds. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:25-32] [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:35]

OpenMausBot has a deterministic cron-to-preset parser (`cronPreset`) covering every day, monthly day, monthly last day, yearly, weekdays, weekly and monthly-nth, plus a sentence renderer (`routineCronText`) that turns a preset into a human line. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/packages/phone-protocol/src/cron-label.ts:9-46] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/server/routine-cron-text.ts:39-42]

Rakazo has the reverse preset-to-cron function (`cronFromPreset`) over the same vocabulary, plus `presetFromCron` and a round-trip test table that pins every preset form to its cron string. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/rakazo-main/packages/core/src/routines/schedule.ts:35-103] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/rakazo-main/packages/core/src/routines/schedule.ts:105-145] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/rakazo-main/packages/core/src/routines/schedule.test.ts:74-96]

Skilled bots' cron reader accepts only five-field cron or a fixed macro set and refuses anything else by name; it never parses natural language, and its output is launchd calendar dictionaries rather than an internal schedule model. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:185-208] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:267-303]

The current definition holds exactly one `trigger` object, and both the installer and slot accounting depend on that: the installer refuses a non-cron trigger with `trigger-not-cron`, and slot accounting refuses any schedule index past zero because "a definition holds one trigger". [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/definition.ts:30-32] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/installer.ts:585-586] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/slot-accounting.ts:208-210]

The smallest planner is a pure `planRoutine(text)` returning `{what, starts[], does, until?}`: a phrase table for the preset vocabulary, a trigger-name table for events, raw-cron passthrough, and an explicit `unparsed` result that falls back to the manual block or a conversation. No model call, no fuzzy matching, no new dependency. Size M because the schema moves from one trigger to a `starts` list; risk medium because installer, slot accounting and status all read `trigger`. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-6]

Event starts need a second, separate change if they must follow the skip policy: an optional `maxLatenessSeconds` on a queued request, checked by the drain against the request's `scheduledFor`, so a mail or pull-request event older than its window is closed as missed instead of run late. Size M, risk medium because it changes the queue's runnable definition. [INFERENCE: based on finding 6]

OpenMausBot's catch-up planner is a stricter explicit rule: the newest occurrence runs late if it is within 12 hours, older occurrences close as missed on one counted row, and late starts found in one scheduler pass are staggered so a long downtime does not start every routine at once. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/server/routine-catch-up.ts:1-20] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenMausBot-main/server/routine-catch-up.ts:23-28]

Queue triggers have no missed-window concept: a request is retried up to three times and then quarantined, and the drain treats every request in the watched folder as runnable, so a stale event is a late run rather than a skipped slot. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-queue.ts:43-46] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/request-drain.ts:12]

Skilled bots already skips missed launchd slots instead of replaying them: the slot-accounting module states that launchd merges every slot a sleeping host missed into one fire, and that each fire names the slot it stood for, how late it ran and which slots it stood in for before dispatch. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/slot-accounting.ts:1-12]

Skilled bots has no 15-minute floor: the cron translator accepts `* * * * *` and turns an all-wildcard minute and hour into `StartInterval 60`, so a bot can fire every minute if its author writes that expression. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:56-57] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/cron-translator.ts:276-280]

Slot accounting classifies lateness as on-time, late or catch-up, with a grace window of half the schedule period clamped between 120 seconds and 7,200 seconds, and summarizes skipped slots under a retention cap. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/slot-accounting.ts:34-47] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/slot-accounting.ts:82-120]

The run record already carries the skipped-slot summary (count, first and last instant, and a capped slot list) and a held-slot reason, so the missed-window evidence is durable without a new store. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/run-record.ts:82-110] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/slot-accounting.ts:38-40]

The smallest change is to enforce the floor at plan or install time by measuring the schedule's shortest gap with the existing `schedulePeriodSeconds` and refusing anything under 900 seconds with a named reason; slot accounting then stays as it is. Size S, risk low. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-5]

OpenBot caps a person at 20 enabled routines because a conversation is an easy place to accumulate standing work without noticing, and switching one off frees a slot. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:113-116]

OpenBot's fatigue rule posts one message on the first failure after a success, switches the routine off after ten consecutive failures with a second final message, and resets the count when a person turns it back on. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/routines.md:118-130]

Skilled bots has neither a per-bot failure streak nor an enabled-bot cap; the only related backoff is the drain job's setup-fault backoff, which protects the drain rather than a bot's schedule. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/installer.ts:89]

The 20-enabled cap belongs at `bots enable` and `bots schedule install`: count enabled definitions or installed schedules and refuse the 21st with a named reason. It is optional for a few people but cheap, and it preserves OpenBot's protection against unnoticed accumulation. Size S, risk low. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1 and 3]

The needs-you store already models one durable operator item per run, and the delivery resolver already routes per-channel entries, so a "switched off after N failures" notice can reuse both. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:1-40] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/delivery.ts:130-171]

The smallest change is a post-run check that counts the last ten terminal run rows for the bot from the status index, and at ten sets a disabled switch with reason `failure-streak` and writes one needs-you item; `bots enable` clears it and resets the count. Size S, risk low because it reads existing rows and writes existing state kinds. [INFERENCE: based on findings 3-6]

The status index already stores one row per run with `botId` and `exitReason`, built only from run records and needs-you items, so a failure streak is a query over existing rows rather than a new store. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status-index.ts:3-14] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status-index.ts:68-88]

The stop-switch layer currently stores only `setAt` for `disabled` and `paused`, so an automatic fatigue stop would be indistinguishable from a person's disable; it needs a reason or a distinct kind so `bots enable` can tell them apart. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/switches.ts:22-29] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/switches.ts:56-76]

Needs-you items are the action-approval analogue for parked runs: a run that needs a human ends, leaves one durable item whose open/answered/expired state is derived from its fields, `bots inbox` lists items and `bots answer` records the answer and enqueues the resume. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:1-10] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:135-212] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/answer.ts:1-14] [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:31] [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:46]

OpenBot decides approval in a fixed order: action kinds first (delete, send, share, post, pay, credentials), then matching rules, then auto-review, then Extra vigilant, with the strictest matching rule winning. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/approvals.md:3-18]

OpenBot defines approvals as the check before an action and activity as the record after it: what was read, changed, sent, refused and approved. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:86-96]

OpenBot recognizes an action by its name, tool name or button label, and treats an app-declared destructive hint from an MCP server, Composio or Arcade as a delete. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/approvals.md:60-84]

OpenBot's card offers four answers: allow once, allow for this conversation, always allow here (saved as a rule), and deny; every answered action still lands on the audit trail. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/approvals.md:20-31]

Skilled bots' existing "approval" is authoring integrity, not action approval: it hashes BOT.md and `bots/config.json` and refuses an unattended run whose bytes differ from what an operator approved at install, enable or manual run. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/approval.ts:1-14]

The smallest terminal approvals inbox is `bots inbox --json` plus the existing answer path, and the smallest activity feed is a `bots activity` verb over the status index's run rows with bot and outcome filters; neither needs a new store. Per-action policy (send, delete, pay) needs a hook inside the executor and is a later packet, with OpenGhost's MIT hook-compatible rules engine as the liftable layer. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-7] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/rules.js:1-10]

The status index already stores one row per run, delivery and item, and `bots status` shows each installed bot's last run and delivery plus open needs-you items, but there is no chronological activity view over those rows. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status-index.ts:1-14] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/status-index.ts:126-133] [SOURCE: .skilled/bin/bots.cjs:48]

A conversation creates a channel and an Intelligence thread, two conversations with the same Bot stay separate, and a Bot's standing role is sent with every run so the job need not be restated. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/coworkers.md:75-80] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/coworkers.md:35-49]

A TUI can carry all four app surfaces from data that already exists: a conversation pane over the new conversation file, an approvals pane over `bots inbox`, an activity pane over the status index, and a routine list over the BOT.md trigger plus schedule state. A desktop shell adds OS notifications, tray and global hotkey, an embedded browser and auto-update, none of which the terminal needs to match the app's information model. [INFERENCE: based on findings 1-7]

OpenBot's conversation is where work is given and reported, can hold more than one Bot, and each Bot takes the part of the work that is its job. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:28-34]

ruledOutDirections.text: Copying Buzz's YAML workflow engine wholesale: it needs a relay, Postgres and a workflow crate, which is far beyond the small-team, terminal-first scope.

Copying OpenBot's server-side sweep and advisory-lock scheduler: skilled bots has no server process and does not need one; launchd, the queue drain and the git hook already provide the firing and single-claim semantics for a small team.
Reading only `routines.md` would have missed the act/tell and until semantics that `how-openbot-works.md` states as the canonical four-part table.

Searching OpenBot's `api/` tree for routine implementation files found only OpenAPI descriptions; the executable routine logic lives in the app and shared packages, so a server-code-only reading would have missed the planner and firing model.

Treating Hermes Muse's fixed six-job table as the target: its fixed cron keys are install-time plumbing, not a user-authored routine surface, and its event intake is limited to cron plus host session hooks.
A license file alone is not enough for OpenMausBot: its `LICENSING.md` carve-out removes `enterprise/` from the Apache grant, which a LICENSE-only reading would have missed.
Adopting OpenBot's Kubernetes charts or managed-upgrade agent for a small team: both solve fleet problems (per-person computers, many installs) that a single host does not have.
Copying OpenMausBot's `enterprise/` code: the directory is outside the Apache-2.0 grant and needs a commercial license for production use.
Lifting openhuman code directly: its GPL-3.0 license would impose copyleft on the combined work, so it is a design reference only.
Reading OpenBot's deployment doc alone would have suggested Kubernetes is the normal path; the minimum-size and single-container sections show the one-host path is fully supported.
Adding a goal store to evaluate outcomes: a single `until` command per routine is enough for a small team, and OpenBot's goal graph is only needed for multi-routine goals.
Evaluating `until` on failed runs: a failed run has no outcome to judge, and treating its failure as "not met" would hide the failure behind a routine continuation.
Looking for an existing post-run hook in the runner found only delivery and worktree cleanup; the terminal path has no outcome-evaluation stage today.
Reusing `precheck` as the until field: it runs before dispatch and its silent marker skips a run, which is the opposite of completing a routine.
Treating the run record's `exit.reason` as an outcome signal would conflate "the run completed" with "the routine's goal is met"; those are different facts and need different fields.
Reading OpenMausBot's `routine-cron-text.ts` as a parser would be wrong: it renders cron to a sentence, and the reverse direction lives in Rakazo's `cronFromPreset`.
Reusing OpenBot's planner directly: `planRoutine` maps form answers to OpenBot's routine/goal/check-in stores, not to skilled bots' trigger union, so only its four-part shape transfers.

Treating every event phrase as a git-hook: only repository events map to the existing hook; mail and other external events need a queue producer, and claiming otherwise would overstate parity.
Using a model to parse routine sentences at run time: it adds nondeterminism and a model call to an authoring step that a closed phrase table can cover.
Adding a new missed-window mechanism for cron: slot accounting already implements skip-not-replay with lateness classes and skipped-slot evidence.
Applying the launchd slot policy to queue requests unchanged: a queue request has no schedule slot, so it needs its own staleness bound rather than the launchd grace window.
Replaying every missed occurrence: both OpenBot and the existing slot accounting explicitly reject a backfill burst.

Treating the drain's retry bound as a missed-window policy would conflate "this attempt failed" with "this occurrence is too old to run"; the two are different facts.
Adding a fatigue counter to each BOT.md definition: the definition is authored state, and the count is runtime history that belongs with run records.
Making the fatigue stop a silent disable: OpenBot posts a final message, and a silent stop would leave a person wondering why the routine stopped.
Reusing the drain backoff as the fatigue rule: the drain backoff protects the drain job from a broken setup, not a bot from a repeating failure.
Searching for existing streak or cap code found only slot-summary and cron-dictionary caps, which bound evidence size rather than bot behavior.
Treating `exitReason` alone as a streak signal would miss refusals that are not failures; the check must count only terminal failed runs.
Adding a new approvals database: needs-you items already model the parked-run question and answer, and the status index already indexes them.
Copying OpenBot's action-recognition table wholesale: it is tuned to browser and app tool names, and skilled bots' executor exposes a different tool surface.
Reusing the definition-approval hash as an action-approval policy: it proves which bytes may run, not which actions a run may take.

Treating `bots status` as an activity feed would lose chronology; it is a snapshot of last run and delivery, not a list of events.
